list.listitem: Suspect Clostridium difficile in any patient with acute watery diarrhea during or shortly after antibiotic therapy. C

When there is a high baseline likelihood of CDI (i.e., hospitalized patient, antibiotic use, no other explanation) order a nucleic acid amplification test as the initial study. If there is a low index of suspicion, begin with toxin ELISA followed by nucleic acid amplification test. C
For an initial nonfulminant episode of CDI, treat with vancomycin or fidaxomicin. For fulminant CDI, use high dose oral or NG administered vancomycin and IV metronidazole. A
For recurrence, do not use the treatment used for the initial episode. Use pulse-tapered vancomycin if fidaxomicin or vancomycin were used initially.B
Fecal microbiota transplant is an option if antibiotic therapy has failed and for patients with recurrences. B

background.definition: Clostridium difficile infection ranges from asymptomatic carrier to severe colitis with toxic megacolon in susceptible patients. Pseudomembranous colitis is the full-blown manifestation of C. difficile colitis, with classic pseudomembranes over the colorectal mucosa.

list.listitem: Hospitals: An estimated three million new cases of C. difficile infection in U.S. hospitals each year.
Community: 6.7/100,000 patients treated with antibiotics.

Healthy adults: up to 10% of patients admitted to the hospital are colonized with toxigenic C. difficile upon admission, with the primary risk factor for colonization being hospitalization within the previous 3 months.
Neonates: 40% colonized.
In 2011 C. difficile was associated with an estimated 4,530,000 infections (66% healthcare-associated) and approximately 29,000 deaths.
Clostridium difficile colonizes the human intestinal tract after the normal gut flora are changed by antibiotic therapy.

After colonization, C. difficile releases two exotoxins, toxin A and toxin B, that bind to receptors on intestinal epithelial cells, causing massive secretion of fluid (diarrhea) and acute inflammation with destruction of epithelial lining and formation of pseudomembranes.
Clostridium difficile infection ranges from asymptomatic carrier to severe colitis with toxic megacolon depending on the host immune response and whether or not the strain is toxigenic.
Infection occurs by the fecal-oral route.
Incidence of community-associated C. difficile infection has been increasing in the last decade (defined as ocurring in pateints not hospitalized in the year prior to diagnosis).
Limit the inappropriate use of antibiotics to decrease the likelihood of outbreaks of C. difficile infection. B

Institute routine infection control measures to prevent C. difficile infection: adhere to hand hygiene procedures between contact with all patients; wear and properly dispose of gloves for patient contact; hand washing preferentially to alcohol-based hand rubs per CDC recommendations; and disinfect objects contaminated with C. difficile with sodium hypochlorite, alkaline glutaraldehyde, or ethylene oxide. A

Once-daily bathing with 2% chlorhexidine cloths is no better at preventing healthcare-associated infections (including CDI) than is bathing with non-antimicrobial cloths in adult patients admitted to the ICU.
Do not attempt to eradicate the carrier state for C. difficile using antibiotics routinely. C

In a secondary prevention trial, using a nontoxigenic C. difficile strain M3 (NTCD-M3) was associated with lower rates of recurrent CDI than placebo (11% vs 30%) after 24 months. The efficacy of prevention was associated with successful colonization with NTCD-M3, which occurred in 69% of treated patients.
American Gastroenterological Association suggest probiotics to prevent C. difficile infection in patients taking antibiotics.
Probiotics containing lactobacilli and Bifidobacteria do not prevent C. difficile infection in hospitalized patients over the age of 65.B
Suspect C. difficile in any patient with acute watery diarrhea during or shortly after antibiotic therapy. C
When there is a high baseline likelihood of CDI (i.e., hospitalized patient, antibiotic use, no other explanation) order a nucleic acid amplification test as the initial study. C
When suspicion for CDI is lower, obtain stool for C. difficile toxins using ELISA followed by a nucleic acid amplification test, or vice versa.C
Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy, when diagnosis in doubt may reveal pseudomembranes. B

Nausea with diarrhea but no fever and negative test for C.difficile toxin
Chronic diarrhea that may be bloody with extraintestinal manifestation; colonoscopic

list.listitem: A diagnosis of pseudomembranous colitis should be considered in patients who present with acute watery diarrhea during or shortly after antibiotic therapy.
Other associated symptoms are crampy lower abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever.
On physical exam, the patient may have abdominal distention, and tenderness.
Patients with fulminant colitis may present as acute abdomen; peritoneal signs suggest perforation.

A prospective study of 217 hospitalized patients who received antibiotics and developed diarrhea A the following as the best independent predictors of positive C. difficile test results: watery diarrhea (OR 17.4), poor functional capacity (OR 9.1), use of proton pump inhibitor (OR 6.1), albumin <2.7 mg/dl (OR 3.8), use of histamine blocker (OR 3.1), and WBC count >13,000 cells/ml (OR 2.7).

Polymerase chain reaction (nucleic acid amplification test) is recommended by IDSA / SHEA guidelines (2018) as the initial single diagnostic test for patients with new, unexplained water diarrhea. If institutional criteria do not limit testing to patients with unexplained diarrhea, a toxin enzyme immunoassay is recommended initially, followed by nucleic acid amplification or vice versa.

Tissue culture cytotoxin assay has been considered the gold standard for diagnosing of C. difficile infection. It may be helpful in large outbreaks. However, it requires a tissue culture facility, which is not widely available in most hospitals and takes 24 to 48 hours to perform.

Stool culture is not specific for toxin-producing bacteria and takes 2 to 5 days. It is only recommended to evaluate selected hospitalized patients whose diarrhea begins within 3 days after admission to identify community-acquired causes of non-C. difficile diarrhea.
Fecal leukocytes: nonspecific, may be absent, not required for the evaluation.
Stool guaiac: positive for occult blood but nonspecific.
CBC with differential: leukocytosis with left shift, as high as 40,000/mm3.
Abdominal X-rays may show dilated colon and ileus patterns.
CT scan of the abdomen: thickened colonic wall and dilatation of the colon.
Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy, when the diagnosis is in doubt, may reveal pseudomembranes.
Aclinical decision rule can predict the likelihood of C. difficile in hospitalized patients.
Consider pseudomembranous colitis in patients with acute watery diarrhea during or shortly after antibiotic therapy and with or without crampy lower abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever.
Obtain stool for C. difficile toxins A and B up to three times using ELISA in a patient with suspected pseudomembranous colitis.
For an initial nonfulminant episode of CDI, treat with vancomycin or fidaxomicin. For fulminant CDI, use high dose oral or NG administered vancomycin and IV metronidazole. A
For recurrence, do not use the treatment used for the initial episode. Use pulse-tapered vancomycin if fidaxomicin or vancomycin were used initially.B
Emergency colectomy for impending colon perforation, severe ileus with megacolon, or refractory septicemia. C
Consider fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) for patients with multiple recurrences or chronic symptoms.B

A small study compared vancomycin liquid with metronidazole in 150 patients with severe pseudomembranous colitis and found a higher cure rate with vancomycin (NNT = 5, 95% CI, 3-27). In addition, in patients with severe Clostridium difficile infection, vancomycin is associated with a lower mortality risk (NNT = 23) compared to metronidazole.
Vancomycin can be administered via nasogastric tube or retention enema in patients who cannot tolerate oral medication or with ileus.

An RCT randomized patients with primary or recurrent C. difficile to the human monoclonal antibody bezlotoxumab or placebo; half took vancomycin, and half took metronidazole. The recurrence rate was lower in the active therapy group (10% reduction, NNT = 10). At a current US cost of $4000, that is about $40,000 to prevent one episode of recurrence. Additional studies are needed to identify which patients are at the greatest risk of recurrence and whether the use could be limited to this subset of high risk patients.

Relapse occurs in 10 to 25 percent of patients treated with metronidazole or vancomycin. The IDSA/SHEA guidelines recommend a different treatment used in the initial episode. For example, if metronidazole was used initially, use vancomycin or fidaxomicin. If vancomycin was used initially, use pulse-tapered vancomycin or fidoxamicin. Pulse tapered vancomycin: 125 mg QID for 1 week, 125 mg BID for 7 days, 125 mg daily for 7 days, 125 mg every other day for 7 days, then 125 mg every 3 days for 14 days.
For the second or subsequent recurrence, use pulse tapered vancomycin or vancomycin for 10 days, followed by rifaximin or fidaxomicin.

A systematic review and network meta-analysis of 24 trials comprising 5361 patients and 13 different treatments concluded that fidaxomicin provides the highest rate of sustained symptomatic cure for CDI, is a better treatment option than vancomycin for all patients except those with severe infections with C difficile, and could be considered as first-line therapy. They also concluded that metronidazole should not be recommended for treatment of C difficile.
Anion-binding resins (cholestyramine, colestipol) have also been used as adjunctive therapy for relapsing infections.
Intravenous immune globulin has been effective in a small number of patients with severe or relapsing infection.

VE303 consists of 8 strains of commensal Clostridia. A trial randomized 79 patients with 1 or more episodes of CDI in the past 6 months to high dose VE303, low-dose VE303 or placebo once daily for 14 days. Recurrence occurred at week 8 in 14% given high-dose, 37% given low-dose, and 46% given placebo (p = 0.006; NNT 3 of high dose vs placebo).

Probiotics are sometimes used for prevention and treatment, but there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against this. A systematic review identified 4 studies, but only one found a reduced risk of recurrence with probiotic. A Cochrane review estimated the NNT is about 65.

A probiotic Lactobacillus preparation (taken twice daily for the course of antibiotics and 7 days afterward) led to an absolute risk reduction of 21.6% (NNT = 5) in the development of any antibiotic-associated diarrhea; no one in the probiotic group developed diarrhea from C. difficile compared with 17% in the placebo group.

In a systematic review with a meta-regression analysis of 19 studies with 6261 subjects, administration of probiotics closer to the first dose of antibiotic reduces the risk of CDI by >50% in hospitalized adults.
Fiber and soy formula reduced the duration of antibiotic-induced diarrhea in children by about one day.
Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) using donor stool has been used in some patients with refractory C. difficille infection.

In patients who have had multiple Clostridium difficile infections (CDIs), FMT (fresh and frozen donor feces, administered by either nasogastric tube or colonoscopy) is associated with a 65% to 80% cure rate with a single treatment and up to 95% cure rate with repeated treatments compared with a ~25% cure rate for antibiotics. The adverse event rate for FMT is 30% (primarily abdominal discomfort); rarely, severe infections (0.7%) and death (0.1%) can occur.

In an RCT of 41 patients, treatment with oral vancomycin (500 mg 4x daily for 14 days) plus large bowel lavage plus an infusion of donor feces was associated with a cure rate of 81.3% compared to 23% to 31% for those receiving vancomycin or vancomycin with lavage.

A systematic review of FMT concluded that it might have substantial short-term effects (resolution of symptoms in up to 81% of treated patients vs. 23% to 31% of patients treated with vancomycin-plus-bowel lavage or vancomycin alone) with few short-term adverse effects.

Among patients with a confirmed diagnosis of CDI who were successfully treated, the administration of nontoxigenix spores of C difficile reduces the rate of recurrent CDI compared to placebo (30% vs. 11%, NNT = 5) over 26 weeks, with fewer study discontinuations due to ADE amongst the active treatment group.

British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines (2024) make a series of recommendations for use of FMT in patients with recurrent CDI. It should be offered to all patients with 2 or more recurrences, following a 10 day course of appropriate antibiotics. Any route of delivery other than enema is acceptable. PPIs and antimotility agents are not recommended prior to FMT, but bowel preparation using polyethylene glycol is recommended. Consider using metoclopramide prior to FMT if administered via the upper GI route. Refer to the guideline for additional detailed recommendations.
Emergency colectomy is recommended for impending colon perforation, severe ileus with megacolon, or refractory septicemia.
Emergency colectomy reduces mortality in some patients with fulminant C. difficile infection.
The recommended surgical procedure is subtotal colectomy with ileostomy, which can be converted to ileorectal anastomosis after colonic inflammation has subsided.
Discontinue ongoing antimicrobial therapy if possible.
Supportive care: correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances.
Avoid antiperistaltic agents (i.e., loperamide and opiates).

The use of antibiotics by a hospitalized patient is associated with a small increased risk of Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) for the subsequent occupant of the same hospital bed (0.72%) vs. 0.43% if the previous occupant did not receive antibiotics, suggesting that antibiotics can alter the local microenvironment enough to influence CDI risk for future patients.
Improvement typically occurs in 3 days with treatment, and virtually all patients recover. B
Relapses occur in 10% to 25% of cases of C. difficile colitis. B
Untreated mortality is 10% to 30%. B
The mortality rate in the untreated is estimated to be 10% to 30%.
With treatment, improvement typically occurs in 3 days and virtually all patients recover.
Relapses occur in 10% to 25% of cases C. difficile colitis.
Patients with at least two previous relapses have about a 65% chance of a subsequent relapse following therapy with vancomycin or metronidazole.
In severely ill patients, colectomy sometimes is required.
Poor prognostic factors include hypoalbuminemia, rapid fall in albumin, over 3 antibiotics, and persistent C. difficile toxin after 7 days of treatment.
Recheck diagnostic studies with each relapse to confirm that C. difficile infection is still the correct diagnosis.
Educate patients about drug therapy, symptoms requiring evaluation, the possibility of relapse, and alternative treatments for the relapse.
The elderly have a higher morbidity and mortality rate from pseudomembranous colitis.
